summary:
Lithuania sets no entry, visa or residence provisions specific to LGBT travellers. No gender-identity question is put at the border, and the immigration rules contain no LGBT-specific screening requirement.

The country has no working procedure for legal gender recognition. Article 5.1 of the Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to change gender through medical intervention, but no implementing legislation has ever been adopted, so the right cannot be exercised through any administrative route. The Lithuanian Gay League described this gap in September 2025 as an 18-year failure of implementation; an LGL item in August 2025 referred to 17 years of legal limbo. Both figures describe the same unimplemented provision.

The Constitutional Court declined in September 2025 to examine a referral from the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court, which in August 2025 had suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and asked the court to rule on the laws' compliance with the Constitution. The refusal left the absence of legal provisions for changing gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents unaddressed by the country's highest court.

The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson's National Review 2024, the second such review after 2019, records the absence of a legal framework and of any strategic approach to trans rights, covering document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes. Reporting in May 2025 documented trans people describing open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse in the workplace, with experts citing systemic labour-market discrimination.

Public assembly protection has a documented failure: in April 2024 the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly, citing an inadequate response to hostile provocators at an LGL assembly, and recommended measures to secure effective assembly rights. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025, covering 2024, records a systemic lack of targeted support for LGBTI hate-crime victims.

Public incitement of violence against LGBT people is explicitly banned under Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code. A 2010 preliminary investigation found that 160 of roughly 180 hate-speech instances, mostly online, concerned the LGBT community; perpetrators were usually fined. Two bills to criminalise 'public propagation of homosexual relations' were rejected by Parliament, in 2011 and 2013.

Expression restrictions targeting minors were struck down: the Constitutional Court ruled on 18 December 2024 that the anti-LGBT provisions of the Law on the Protection of Minors violated Article 25, freedom of speech. The ECHR Grand Chamber had ruled in January 2023 that the 2014 Ministry of Culture ban on a children's book involving same-sex relationships violated Article 10. Pride events have been repeatedly obstructed: a court halted Baltic Pride 2010 shortly before it began, overturned one day prior, and the march proceeded under heavy policing with 12 arrests; the 2013 march required litigation through all judicial instances, drawing about 500 participants and 28 arrests. Participation has since grown, to around 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and around 5,000 in 2023.

Marriage is limited to opposite-sex couples by Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code. On 17 April 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions, including for same-sex couples, contradicts the Constitution, and granted same-sex couples the right to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive registered-partnership law. In January 2019 the Constitutional Court ruled that foreign same-sex spouses must be granted residence permits, following the 2018 ECJ ruling in Coman. Adoption remains closed to same-sex couples because marriage is required; single gay applicants are in practice not able to adopt.

A 2013 parliamentary package included a proposed ban on gender reassignment on the stated basis that 'gender is determined genetically from the very moment of conception', alongside fines up to €1,800 for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values'. The inventory does not record the outcome of that specific bill. ILGA-Europe's 2025 review notes the prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule was complicated by his MEP immunity.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal since 1993. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 and raised to 16 on 2 July 2010 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
The 2013 five-bill package and the 2011 and 2013 'public propagation' bills show a recurring legislative pattern of proposed restrictions on trans and LGBT life, though the inventory records the propagation bills as rejected and does not record the fate of the gender-reassignment ban bill.

Public hostility has a documented institutional footprint: more than 10,000 people protested against partnership legislation in Vilnius in May 2021, and President Gitanas Nauseda stated in September 2021 he would do his best to block adoption demands from Kaunas Pride organisers. A partnership bill was preliminarily approved 46–17 in May 2017 but remained pending as of 2019.

ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon were granted protection after a four-year wait amid dire camp conditions, and that a psychologist was convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts. This concerns the asylum system rather than visitor entry.

Only 24 same-sex households were declared in the 2011 census, a figure that predates the 2024 partnership ruling and reflects the pre-recognition legal position rather than current household composition.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not record the outcome of the 2013 bill proposing a ban on gender reassignment, only that parliament was to consider it alongside four other anti-gay and anti-trans bills.

Whether the Seimas has acted on the Ombudsperson's April 2024 assembly-protection recommendations is not sourced here.

The current status of the partnership bill first preliminarily approved in 2017, and whether a comprehensive registered-partnership law has been adopted since the April 2025 ruling, are unresolved in this inventory.

No trans-specific killing or violence rate for Lithuania appears in the inventory, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made.

The 2011 census figure of 24 same-sex households is historical and predates both the 2019 residence-permit ruling and the 2025 partnership ruling.
